coverageNote: Enumerated from disk: 8 units (the domain directory itself plus 7 sub-domain directories, each containing an *-index.md), 48 files total — matches the expected 8 units / 48 files exactly. Every file was read in full (05.03.05 and 05.06.03 in two pages each because of size). No sampling. Dimensions 1 (Problem Clarity) and 4 (Constraint Explicitness) are marked N/A on every unit: both belong to meta/problem-statement.md and meta/constraints.md, which are outside this domain's tree, and scoring them here would either flatter (auto-✅) or penalise absence of something never in scope. Dimension 6 (Competitive Positioning) is applicable only to the domain root, which names SoundBetter, AirGigs and Fiverr Pro with a specific capability gap and a defensible moat; it is N/A on sub-domain units per the rubric's own note. Dimension 5 is scored as applicable because these files are unusually numeric (3 rounds, 48h notes window, 14-day expiry, 45-day abandonment, 60s clips, >=5 sellers/90 days, 100ms duration tolerance, -90 dBFS silence) and several decisions state explicitly that thresholds are given concretely so they are testable.

findings.claim: Silent contradiction on whether the seller's concurrency ceiling blocks quote ISSUANCE. The domain CX resolves the capacity/immutable-offer collision by making the cap gate issuance; 05.02.01 explicitly rejects any gate and resolves the same collision as display-only legibility. Both are presented as the resolution of the same conflict (CX-12 / DT-04), neither carries a marker, and they give opposite behaviour for a seller at capacity who tries to quote.
findings.evidence: services-marketplace-cx.md:23 — "**Capacity ceiling vs immutable offer** ... Resolved: the cap gates quote *issuance*, not acceptance."; services-marketplace-cx.md:137 — "issuance of a *new* quote is what the ceiling blocks. Failure surfaces at issuance (\"you're at capacity\"), never at the buyer's acceptance."; services-marketplace-cx.md:139 — "The seller is warned at issuance when near capacity". CONTRADICTED BY 05.02.01-custom-quotes-proposals-scope.md:170 (DT-04) — "(a) an issued quote **reserves** a concurrency slot — fails immediately ... The design obligation is therefore not a gate but **legibility**: show the seller their live-offer exposure in workload terms at the moment of issue, and let expiry (D-04) do the reaping." and 05.02.01:112 — "The ceiling binds *ordering* (05.01.07 D-03), not acceptance." 05.01.07-seller-capacity-queue-intake-limits.md:94 (D-03) covers only orderability — "At-capacity listings stay visible and non-orderable" — and no edge case in that file mentions quote issuance at all.
findings.failure_scenario: A mix engineer with a ceiling of 3 has 3 engagements in flight. A fourth buyer requests a quote. Implementer A follows the domain CX and blocks issuance with "you're at capacity", so the seller cannot quote work that starts in six weeks and the buyer is turned away with no offer. Implementer B follows 05.02.01 DT-04, issues the quote and shows the seller "4 live quotes totalling 18 days against a ceiling of 3". The two builds differ on whether a busy seller can transact at all, and each cites a decision in the tree as its authority.

findings.claim: The Carried Terms table is declared normative and exhaustive-by-intent — a term absent from it "is not agreed, is not enforceable, and is not measurable" — and it omits the post-delivery recall/support window, which 05.03.06 requires to be a bounded, per-craft commercial term. It also omits the trial scope that this same file's own D-17 calls "a first-class quote term". By the file's own stated rule, 05.03.06's entire bounding mechanism is unagreed.
findings.evidence: 05.02.01-custom-quotes-proposals-scope.md:35 — "Every term below is agreed *here* or is not agreed at all."; 05.02.01:14 — "A term that is not on the accepted version is not agreed, is not enforceable, and is not measurable — which makes an omission here a silent failure in a sibling feature."; 05.02.01:236 (D-07) — "The breadth pass's list omitted the kill-fee schedule ... the anonymity level ... and the milestone structure — each an omission that would silently disable a sibling. An enumerated table is the only defence." The table (05.02.01:37-58) lists 20 terms and contains no recall/support window row and no trial-scope row. REQUIRED BY 05.03.06-post-delivery-support-recall.md:89 (D-03) — "The window is bounded in both duration and count" — and 05.03.06:99 (Q-04) — "Default window length per craft?", plus 05.02.01:246 (D-17) — "A **trial scope** is a first-class quote term".
findings.failure_scenario: A quote is issued and accepted with no recall window stated because the normative term list never asked for one. Three months later the buyer's mastering engineer finds a spitting hi-hat and requests a recall. The seller says the window closed; the buyer says no window was ever agreed. 05.03.06 D-03 requires a bound in duration and count, the accepted quote carries neither, and by 05.02.01 D-07's own rule there is nothing enforceable to measure the request against. The same omission means an implementer building the quote surface has no field in which to put the recall window and must invent where it is declared.

findings.claim: Silent contradiction on whether a seller-fault cancellation can create any payment obligation. D-20 states there is never one; D-13 caps a party's liability at the engagement value and the on-location edge cases render that cap to the buyer as the seller's exposure, with a declared higher cap ("date guarantee") as a priced instrument. A cap of GBP 400 on an obligation that D-20 says can never exist is not satisfiable.
findings.evidence: 05.03.05-cancellation-abandonment-kill-fee.md:288 (D-20) — "There is **no reverse kill fee**. A seller's fault produces refund + cover + a reputation fact, **never a payment obligation**"; 05.03.05:84 — "**Seller-fault, both models: zero.** There is no reverse kill fee (D-20)." CONTRADICTED BY 05.03.05:281 (D-13) — "A party's liability on cancellation is **capped at the engagement value** unless the quote declares a higher cap"; 05.03.05:169 — "The seller's liability is **capped at the engagement value** (D-13). A GBP 400 drummer does not owe a GBP 2,000 studio ... | At booking: \"{Seller}'s liability is capped at GBP 400. Your room deposit is not covered.\""; 05.03.05:170 — "Quote declared a higher liability cap (a \"date guarantee\") | The declared cap governs. Real in artist contracts and priced accordingly."; DT-12 (05.03.05:234) argues the whole case in terms of the seller's liability exposure — "Unbounded consequential liability means a GBP 400 engagement carries GBP 2,000 of risk".
findings.failure_scenario: A session drummer cancels an on-location date 5 days out. The buyer's studio booking is non-refundable at GBP 2,000. Implementer A applies D-20 and the seller owes nothing: the settlement shows full refund of unsettled escrow, seller expenses reimbursed, zero to the buyer. Implementer B applies D-13 and the seller owes up to the GBP 400 engagement value, which is exactly what the buyer was told at booking time. The buyer has been shown a cap that one build honours and the other treats as a nullity, and the platform has published a liability figure it may not charge.

findings.claim: The taxonomy's axis table fixes rights posture at "Exactly 1" per listing and cites, as its authority, the very decision that makes the election per-tier and states that tiers routinely differ. A three-tier listing whose tiers elect different postures cannot satisfy both statements, and the publish gate that blocks on a missing tier-2 posture is unimplementable against a single listing-level field.
findings.evidence: 05.01.02-service-category-taxonomy-attributes.md:44 — "| Rights posture | work-for-hire · licence · co-ownership · points | `05.06.01` | **Exactly 1** | Always (`05.01.01` D-02 — no default) |" under the column header "Cardinality on a listing" (05.01.02:35). CONTRADICTED BY 05.01.01-service-listings-packages-rate-cards.md:183 (D-02) — "Rights posture is an explicit election **per tier** at publish time — no default ... **Per tier rather than per listing** because tiers routinely differ in what they hand over"; 05.01.01:74 — "Seller elects posture on tier 1 but not tier 2 | Publish blocked — election is per **tier**, not per listing. A \"Mix\" tier licensing the mix and a \"Mix + Stems\" tier assigning it are different deals."; and 05.06.01-engagement-rights-posture.md:34 — "There are **two elections per tier**, because there are two copyrights" (which makes the true per-listing cardinality 2 x number-of-tiers, not 1).
findings.failure_scenario: A producer publishes a listing with tiers Mix (licence), Mix + Master (assignment) and Mix + Master + Stems (assignment + composition co-ownership). The implementer builds posture as the taxonomy says — one value per listing — so the publish gate cannot detect that tier 2 has no posture, the facet index records one posture for a listing that grants three different things, and buyers browsing by posture are shown a listing whose actual grant depends on which tier they order.

findings.claim: The quote's ordered price evaluation does not say whether multiple percentage add-ons compound. The model is named percentage-of-subtotal (implying each is computed against the same subtotal, making order irrelevant) while the step says they are applied "in declared order" (implying a running total, where order is the only thing that matters) and the two worked examples use incompatible notations (+50% and x1.5).
findings.evidence: 05.01.01-service-listings-packages-rate-cards.md:38 — "4. **Percentage add-ons** — applied to the subtotal in declared order (rush +50% per 05.01.06; Atmos x1.5)."; 05.01.01:43 — "An add-on's pricing model is restricted to `{flat, same-unit-as-tier, percentage-of-subtotal}`."; 05.01.01:184 (D-03) — "The order matters because percentage add-ons must compose on the subtotal" — which asserts both that order matters and that composition is on the subtotal.
findings.forcedInvention: Whether the Nth percentage add-on is computed against the frozen subtotal or against the running total after the (N-1)th.
findings.failure_scenario: Subtotal GBP 2,000 with rush +50% and Atmos x1.5. Non-compounding: 2,000 + 1,000 + 1,000 = GBP 4,000 fee total. Compounding in declared order: 2,000 x 1.5 x 1.5 = GBP 4,500. The two implementations differ by GBP 500 on one quote, and the figure is the take-rate base (step 5), so the platform's own revenue and the seller's contracted fee both diverge.

findings.claim: The universal-parameter rule and the per-model required-parameter table disagree about what a zero-cash model must declare before publish. The universal rule binds every model "regardless of shape" and makes a model missing any of them unpublishable; the Points and Spec rows list no minimum, currency, tax treatment or rounding rule; and D-04 narrows only two of the four to cash models, leaving minimum (D-03) and rounding (D-05) unqualified.
findings.evidence: 05.01.03-music-pricing-model-library.md:49 — "Every model — regardless of shape — declares these before it can be published. A model missing any of them is **not publishable**; the listing cannot go live (D-03, D-04, D-05)" over the rows Minimum / Currency / Tax treatment / Rounding rule (05.01.03:51-56). CONTRADICTED BY the model table's required-parameter cells: Points — "percentage · **asset (master / publishing / both)**" (05.01.03:42), Spec — "**trigger condition** · the term that vests on trigger · **the elected posture whose effect it defers**" (05.01.03:43). D-04 (05.01.03:186) says "Every **cash** model declares **currency and tax treatment**", but D-03 (05.01.03:185) says "**Every** model declares a **minimum**; a model without one is not publishable" and D-05 (05.01.03:187) leaves rounding unscoped.
findings.forcedInvention: Whether the publish gate demands a minimum, a currency, a tax treatment and a rounding rule on a points-only or spec listing, and if so what a 'minimum' or 'rounding rule' means for a percentage of a master.
findings.failure_scenario: A topline writer publishes a points-only listing (3 points on the master, composition co-ownership). Implementer A applies the universal rule literally: publish is blocked pending a minimum and a rounding rule that cannot sensibly be given for a royalty percentage, so points-only listings cannot go live at all — silently removing the deal shape the domain flags as its most exploitation-prone. Implementer B applies the per-model table and publishes with two parameters. The publish gate is the difference between a market segment existing and not existing.

findings.claim: The waitlist release rule is stated twice with incompatible mechanics: the Behavior section specifies a sequential, one-at-a-time offer with a bounded conversion window and explicitly rejects a race, while the Happy Path specifies that the first buyer to convert takes the slot.
findings.evidence: 05.01.07-seller-capacity-queue-intake-limits.md:32 — "**Waitlist as an ordered queue, not a scramble.** When a slot frees, the platform notifies waitlisted buyers **in join order**, one at a time, each with a bounded window to convert (Level-1 default: 24h) before the offer passes to the next. **It is not a first-to-click free-for-all**, because that punishes the buyer who was there first and rewards whoever happens to be online." CONTRADICTED BY 05.01.07:42 (Happy Path step 5) — "Waitlisted buyers are notified in order; **the first to convert takes the slot**."
findings.failure_scenario: A slot frees on a seller with four waitlisted buyers. Implementer A reads the Happy Path and notifies all four at once; the buyer who joined fourth happens to be at their desk and takes the slot, which is the outcome the Behavior section says the design exists to prevent. Implementer B offers to buyer 1 with a 24h window. The two builds differ on who gets the work and on how many notifications fire.

findings.claim: The capacity ceiling's stated rationale (one human has one finite week across all their crafts) does not support the decision it is attached to (a separate ceiling per craft), and nothing anywhere caps a multi-hyphenate's aggregate concurrent load — which is the order-bombing failure the feature exists to prevent. No open question covers the gap.
findings.evidence: 05.01.07-seller-capacity-queue-intake-limits.md:17 — "Critically for the multi-hyphenate: the ceiling is **per human, not per listing** — a drummer selling session work, mixing and repair from one account **has one finite week**."; 05.01.07:93 (D-02) — "The ceiling is **per human per craft**, not per listing | The multi-hyphenate has one finite week regardless of how many listings they publish." The four open questions (05.01.07:100-103) cover remote-vs-on-location reconciliation, the default value, rush slot cost and inferred capacity — none covers cross-craft aggregate load. DT-02 (05.01.07:74) states the harm the ceiling exists to prevent: "a well-reviewed engineer ranks up, receives more orders, breaches turnaround (05.01.06), gets worse reviews, and the platform has manufactured the failure by rewarding them."
findings.failure_scenario: A multi-hyphenate sells session drums, mixing and gear repair with the default ceiling of 3 on each craft. They accept 3 mixes, 3 remote overdub sessions and 3 repairs — 9 concurrent engagements, every craft reporting Available, every ceiling respected, and the seller in exactly the over-committed state the feature was created to prevent. No rule in the tree stops it and no question records it as open.

findings.claim: The Delayed anonymity level — described as the most common real case — is keyed to a release event that this domain establishes elsewhere it cannot observe, and 05.02.02 records no question, no owner and no cross-reference for who detects the release. The backstop rule makes the dependency worse: it requires the platform to know at backstop expiry that the material is still unreleased.
findings.evidence: 05.02.02-nda-confidentiality-ghost-production.md:36 — "| Delayed | Named after an embargo (**release date + N**), with a required backstop | Full | Unreleased material, standard |"; 05.02.02:48 (Happy Path 7) — "On embargo expiry (Delayed), the credit surfaces automatically"; 05.02.02:60 — "Delayed embargo's release never happens (track shelved) ... rather than auto-publishing a credit against unreleased material, the credit **converts to Sealed**". The same class of dependency is treated as blocking elsewhere: 05.01.03-music-pricing-model-library.md:206 (Q-07) — "**[PREREQUISITE — blocking, promoted 2026-07-30]** A spec deal's vesting trigger (\"the song was cut\") is an event in domain 12 that this domain cannot observe (DT-10). **Who detects the trigger and notifies the spec engagement**". 05.02.02's Cross-Cut Notes (lines 95-105) list 02, 09, 10, 24 and four cross-cuts — domain 12 is absent — and its four open questions (lines 122-125) cover posture conflict, counter-attestation, the default backstop window and DSAR, none of them release detection.
findings.failure_scenario: A ghost-written single is delivered under a Delayed election with a 12-month backstop. The track is released in month 4. Nothing in the tree says what observes that release, so the credit does not surface on release + N; it sits until the backstop fires at month 12 and then converts to Sealed on the reasoning that no release occurred — permanently hiding a credit both parties agreed would publish, on the platform's most common anonymity level.

findings.claim: The mixed union / non-union session case is marked as a real and messy case, given no behaviour, and deferred with a marker that names no owner and points at a pass the domain declares complete. No open question in 05.02.03 or the sub-domain index covers it, so nothing downstream will pick it up.
findings.evidence: 05.02.03-union-session-contracting.md:48 — "| Non-union player on a union date, or vice versa | A mixed session is a real and messy case | `[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]` |" — no owner column entry, and no corresponding row in that file's Open Questions (05.02.03:96-99, which cover scale-table sourcing, new-use obligations, the non-signatory buyer and launch jurisdictions) or in 05.02-quotes-scope-contracting-index.md:51-53. The named target is declared finished: services-marketplace-cx.md:5 — "**Status**: [DEEP] — 7 sub-domains, **deepening pass complete**".
findings.failure_scenario: A producer books a five-piece where three players are AFM members and two are not. The quote elects union terms. An implementer must invent whether the scale floor applies to the whole engagement, per player, or blocks issue — and 05.05.02 D-04 ("Union scale applies per player, not to the fixer's aggregate fee") only settles the fixer case, not the mixed-membership case. Whichever is chosen, no owner is recorded as having chosen it.

findings.claim: The auto-accept window's business-days rule answers an open product question in the same sentence in which it forbids itself from answering it. 05.01.06 Q-02 is unresolved and owner-assigned, but 05.04.01's control table states the answer as fact, so an implementer reads a decided rule where the owner still holds a live choice.
findings.evidence: 05.04.01-delivery-acceptance-auto-accept.md:56 — "| **Business days** | **The seller's jurisdiction's**, per 05.01.06 Q-02, which owns this question. This feature inherits whatever that resolves to and **must not answer it independently** |". CONTRADICTED BY 05.01.06-turnaround-rush-service-levels.md:105 (Q-02) — "Are \"working days\" the seller's jurisdiction's or the buyer's? They differ, and the answer determines who absorbs a bank holiday. | User | Step 5 deepening" — still open, owner User. 05.04.01:191 repeats the inheritance obligation: "The window inherits its absolute-date rendering (D-03) and its business-days definition (Q-02). This feature must not answer the working-days question independently."
findings.failure_scenario: A US buyer receives a mix from a UK seller on the Friday before the late-May bank holiday. The 7-business-day window resolves to a different absolute deadline under each jurisdiction. The implementer codes the seller's jurisdiction because 05.04.01 states it; the owner later rules for the buyer's jurisdiction on 05.01.06 Q-02, and every auto-accept deadline already computed and shown to buyers as a fixed instant (D-13) is wrong by a day, on a timer whose expiry executes a copyright assignment.

findings.claim: The terminated-seller edge case says the money leg "holds" while rights and credit execute, using the same term the feature's own leg table defines as escrow release. Read literally it breaks the all-three-or-none rule and produces the outcome the feature calls the worst it could produce; read as a payout hold it is consistent with 05.06.03's ledger/rail split. Nothing in 05.04.01 distinguishes the two.
findings.evidence: 05.04.01-delivery-acceptance-auto-accept.md:119 — "**Seller's account terminated during the window** | Buyer may still accept ... Rights and credit execute; **the money leg holds pending resolution rather than failing the commit**". The leg table defines the term: 05.04.01:35 — "| Money | Payments, Escrow & Payouts cross-cut | Escrow releases to the seller", and 05.04.01:39 — "All three, or none (D-02)." DT-02 names the consequence: 05.04.01:171 — "Rights transfer succeeds, escrow release fails: the seller has assigned their copyright and not been paid, which is the single worst outcome the platform could produce". The resolving distinction exists only in a sibling unit: 05.06.03-rights-transfer-split-execution.md:236 (D-06) — "**The ledger is in the commit; the payment rail is not.**" — and that file's analogous row (05.06.03:139) says "Rights and credit **execute**; the **payout** is held", using the word 05.04.01 does not.
findings.failure_scenario: A seller's account is terminated during the auto-accept window; the buyer accepts. An implementer working from 05.04.01 alone defers the escrow release and commits rights plus credit, so the buyer owns the master, the credit graph records it, and the funds stay in the buyer's held balance — an executed assignment with no payment, which is precisely what D-02 exists to make impossible.

findings.claim: QC's fail-open posture lets the auto-accept clock start on a file nothing verified, which falsifies the guarantee the sub-domain's own D-02 gives. The conflict is named in the tree but carries no owner, no open question and no deferral target beyond a synthesis pass the domain declares finished.
findings.evidence: 05.04-delivery-qc-acceptance-index.md:46 (D-02) — "QC gates **delivery**, not acceptance | A technically broken file must never reach the buyer and start their auto-accept clock." and 05.04.02-deliverable-spec-automated-audio-qc.md:27 — "a failing file is rejected back to the seller and the buyer never sees it, **so their auto-accept clock never starts on a file that was never valid**." CONTRADICTED BY 05.04.02:107 (D-05) — "When the engine is unavailable, **fail open with a visible flag**" and acknowledged without ownership at 05.04.01-delivery-acceptance-auto-accept.md:183 — "QC's fail-open posture (D-05) means a window can run on an unchecked-but-flagged file — which is deliberate but **worth Step 6's attention**, because auto-accept on a flagged file transfers rights over a deliverable nobody verified." No question in 05.04.01 (Q-01..Q-06), 05.04.02 (Q-01..Q-03) or the sub-domain index (Q-01..Q-03) records it, and services-marketplace-cx.md:5 declares the synthesis pass complete.
findings.failure_scenario: The DSP service is down for two hours. Three deliveries publish unchecked-but-flagged. A buyer on tour never opens theirs; seven business days later auto-accept fires, executing a copyright assignment and releasing escrow over a 44.1k master where 48k was the agreed spec — the exact scenario 05.04.02 DT-02 describes as the reason QC gates delivery. Nobody owns the decision about whether the clock may run in that state.

findings.claim: Multi-party settlement needs a per-payee escrow freeze when one downstream sub-engagement is disputed, but the only rule stated anywhere for a dispute freezes the whole escrow. The requirement is recorded twice as a bare [PENDING] with no owner, no deferral stage and no corresponding open question in either index.
findings.evidence: 05.05-multi-party-supply-cx.md:73 — "A downstream engagement disputed while the buyer's acceptance fires. The buyer's release should not be held hostage to a dispute between the fixer and one player — but the disputed player's tranche must be. **Needs a per-payee freeze rather than a whole-escrow freeze; `[PENDING]`**."; the identical marker at services-marketplace-cx.md:104 — "needing a **per-payee freeze**, not a whole-escrow freeze. `[PENDING]`". The only stated behaviour is whole-escrow: 05.04.01-delivery-acceptance-auto-accept.md:133 — "Buyer disputes rather than accepts | **Escrow frozen**; routed to domain 24. Nothing transfers while frozen." Neither 05.05-multi-party-supply-index.md:53-55 nor 05.05.02-fixers-ensemble-contracting.md:102-104 lists it as a question, and 05.05.02 D-02 asserts the settlement shape without a freeze rule.
findings.failure_scenario: A fixer's twelve-piece date settles from one escrow release. One player disputes their fee with the fixer the day the buyer accepts. An implementer applies the only stated rule and freezes the escrow, so eleven players who did nothing wrong are unpaid and the buyer's acceptance cannot complete — the profession's oldest failure (05.05.02 DT-03) reproduced by the mechanism built to end it.

findings.claim: Whether an executed points participation survives a later re-recording of the work is marked [PENDING] with no owner, no deferral stage and no open question, in a feature whose whole product is a participation that pays out for decades.
findings.evidence: 05.06.02-producer-points-backend-participation.md:62 — "| Points on a recording later re-recorded | The 2020s' favourite manoeuvre | `[PENDING]` |" — bare marker, no stage, no owner. The file's four open questions (05.06.02:122-125) cover points-only leverage, blocking an unauthorised grant, where the aggregate check lives, and expected-value disclosure; none covers re-recording. The stakes are stated by the file itself: 05.06.02:113 (D-02) — "Points elected here must **execute** into 09/10 at acceptance" and 05.06.02:48 — "Royalties flow from 10 for as long as the recording earns".
findings.failure_scenario: A producer takes 3 master points on a 2027 recording. In 2032 the artist re-records the song to escape a label deal. An implementer must invent whether the participation attaches to that master only (the producer earns nothing from the version now being streamed) or follows the composition (which would silently convert a master participation into a publishing one). Nobody is recorded as owning the choice, and 09/10 will build against whichever guess ships.

findings.claim: Two custodial race conditions are identified and left with a bare [PENDING] — no owner, no stage, no open question — while every structurally identical race elsewhere in the domain is resolved with an explicit precedence decision.
findings.evidence: 05.07-custodial-physical-services-cx.md:41 — "Damage discovered at return while the job is still marked in progress; or a revised estimate issued while the item is already being returned. **Both need a defined precedence; `[PENDING]`**." No question in 05.07.01 (Q-01..Q-04), 05.07.03 (Q-01..Q-04) or the sub-domain index (Q-01..Q-03) covers either. Compare the resolved analogues: 05.03.05-cancellation-abandonment-kill-fee.md:284 (D-16) — "**Delivery wins** a race with cancellation"; 05.05.01-deps-substitutes-emergency-cover.md:112 (D-05) — precedence at "the buyer's recorded approval"; 05.04.01-delivery-acceptance-auto-accept.md:213 (D-04) — the 120-second grace.
findings.failure_scenario: A luthier ships a refretted guitar back and, the same afternoon, discovers and reports a crack that happened on the bench. The job ticket still reads In Progress and the custody chain has already moved to In Transit (return). An implementer must invent whether the damage record attaches to the workshop leg or the carrier leg — which decides whether the claim is against the seller or the carrier's insurance, on the sub-domain's highest-value dispute type.

findings.claim: The domain's own status metadata is internally inconsistent and, as a consequence, roughly a dozen tracked deferrals across the tree point at a pass that the domain CX declares finished. The Children table reports every sub-domain as [BREADTH] while their indexes report their children at [DEEP], [PARTIAL] and [SURFACE]; the CX simultaneously claims the deepening pass is complete while 15 of the 32 leaf files are not [DEEP].
findings.evidence: services-marketplace-index.md:5 — "**Status**: [BREADTH]" and the Children table (services-marketplace-index.md:33-39) marking all seven sub-domains "`[BREADTH]`". CONTRADICTED BY services-marketplace-cx.md:5 — "**Status**: [DEEP] — 7 sub-domains, **deepening pass complete**" and by the actual child statuses, e.g. 05.01-service-listings-pricing-index.md:18-24 ([DEEP] x3, [PARTIAL] x4), 05.02-quotes-scope-contracting-index.md:20 ("[SURFACE]"), 05.05-multi-party-supply-index.md:19-21 ([SURFACE] x3), 05.07-custodial-physical-services-index.md:18-20 ([SURFACE] x3).
